# Diagnosing Variable Chain Tension on a Sidecar Motorcycle

If your motorcycle chain behaves differently depending on whether you push it forward in gear or roll it backward, the issue is almost certainly mechanical alignment rather than simple wear. In the specific case of a Yamaha XJ600 with a sidecar, this "tight when pushed, loose when rolled" symptom points directly to the geometry of the rear axle and sprocket mounting.

When you push the bike forward in gear (with the clutch pulled in), you are essentially applying a tensile load to the chain similar to driving under load. This tension pulls the rear wheel straight relative to the frame if there is significant play in the swingarm or axle bearings. Conversely, when you roll the bike backward or let it sit in neutral, gravity and the weight distribution shift allow any existing lateral play to manifest as slack. The fact that the chain is loose even when rolled forward in neutral suggests the rear wheel has excessive axial (in-and-out) or vertical (up-and-down) play, or the rear sprocket itself is damaged.

### Axle Bearing Play and Wheel Alignment

The most common culprit in this scenario is worn axle bearings or a loose axle nut. On many motorcycles, including the XJ600 family, the rear wheel is mounted on tapered roller bearings. If these bearings have developed clearance, the wheel can move slightly side-to-side within the swingarm pivot point.

When you push forward against the drive train, this force compresses the chain and masks the lateral movement of the wheel. However, once that driving force is removed, the wheel returns to its resting position, which might be skewed if the bearings are worn. This creates an illusion of a loose chain because the rear sprocket is no longer perfectly aligned with the front sprocket.

To verify this without removing the wheel:
1.  Lift the rear wheel off the ground.
2.  Grasp the tire at the 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock positions.
3.  Attempt to rock the wheel in and out (axial play) and up and down (vertical play).

If you feel significant movement, the axle bearings need replacement or adjustment. This is a critical safety step before tightening the chain, as overtightening a chain on a misaligned wheel places uneven stress on the rollers and plates, accelerating wear and increasing the risk of failure.

### Inspecting the Rear Sprocket

The source material mentions fitting a new rear sprocket recently. While unlikely to be the cause immediately after installation, it is worth inspecting for "dogtooth" or chipped teeth. If the sprocket has missing teeth, the chain will jump slightly as it engages and disengages, creating slack and noise.

Because of the sidecar attachment, accessing the front sprocket and rear axle area can be physically awkward. This makes visual inspection difficult without removing the wheel. If the bike refuses to be lifted easily or requires significant force to rotate the wheel by hand after bearing replacement, you may need to remove the wheel to inspect the bearings' rollers directly.

### The Danger of Overtightening

The hesitation to tighten the chain is valid. A chain that is too tight can strip splines from the sprockets, damage swingarm pivot bearings, or snap due to excessive tension. However, a chain that is loose under load (which happens if you ignore this issue) will slap against the frame and sidecar chassis, causing structural damage and loss of control.

The correct approach is to address the root cause: alignment and bearing play. Once the rear wheel is seated firmly in the swingarm with no detectable axle play, adjust the chain tensioner (usually a bolt on the left side or top bracket) until there is approximately 30mm of vertical free play at the midpoint of the run. Re-check this after a short ride to ensure the bearings hold the alignment.

If the wheel remains misaligned even after bearing adjustment, the rear sprocket mounting flange might be bent, or the swingarm pivot bushings could be worn. In these cases, replacing the affected components is necessary to restore safe chain tension before riding again.
